new_statements.citation: one of the works listed for this language (see the verification note)
new_statements.check: reported on verification, not yet confirmed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Spot-checked all four 'silent' supplementary works (JIPA ms, Bossers & Boone 2023, NLLT preprint + NLLT text, balafon paper) by a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|prominen|intonation|metrical|foot|feet|tonic: none says anything about word stress in Northern Toussian; the only hits are Bossers & Boone's tone-diacritic sentence (p. 8), the NLLT metrical-grid analogy (preprint p. 29) and 'intonational boundary tones'. Nothing missed for nort2787. The only stress-adjacent remark anywhere held by the project is Prost 1964's 'position inaccentuée' / 'ə atone' vowel-reduction note, which concerns Southern Toussian (wib) and was correctly excluded.

tone_statements.citation: Struthers-Young, Anthony. 2026 (ms dated May 7, 2026). Northern Toussian. Submitted to Journal of the International Phonetic Association (JIPA Illustration; Djigouera dialect). 38 pp. lingbuzz/010271
tone_statements.quote: Tonology • Tonal inventory • three contrastive level tones: H á, M ā, L à • three two-tone contour tones: HM a᷇, HL â, LH ǎ • three three-tone contour tones: HLH â´, LHL ǎ`, LHM ǎ¯ ... Automatic downstep • There is automatic downstep (downdrift) where lower tones cause downstep of higher tones • L triggers downstep of following M and H (3a-b) • M triggers downstep of following H (3c) • A downstepped H has a higher pitch than a M
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones H/M/L; six contours listed as two-/three-tone combinations (not counted as tonemes); non-automatic downstep from two floating Ls can apply twice; pitch tracks in Hz shown.

tone_statements.quote: Northern Toussian is Niger Congo language of Burkina Faso • Complex tone system with three tone levels • Multiple sources of downstep • Automatic downstep • Several constructions that condition non-automatic downstep • Natural classes of tones that condition registral effects • L and M trigger automatic downstep • M and H are targeted by automatic downstep ... Tonal inventory (3) H jí ‘year’ M jī ‘laughter’ L jì ‘hair’ HM dɛ᷇ˤ ‘dream (N)’ HL dɛ̂ˤ ‘stone’ LH bǒ ‘father’ HLH bê´ ‘again’ LHL sɔ̰`̌ ‘comportment’ LHM lɛ̰¯̌ ‘maternal uncles’

Handout/slides linked from the author's CV page (https://www.anthonystruthersyoung.com/static/homepage/documents/acal_2024.pdf).
tone_statements.quote: Northern Toussian has three level tones: a high tone (á), mid tone (ā), and low tone (à). Additionally, it has six lexical contour tones, HM (a᷇ ), HL (â), LH (ǎ), LHL (ǎ`), LHM (ǎ¯), and HLH (â´), though the HLH contour is only attested in one word, bê´ ‘again.’ I analyze the contour tones as being comprised of two or more of the level tones. … Downstep is frequent in the language, and both H and M tones can be downstepped.

tone_statements.quote: Basic Tonology 3 tone system • H, M, L, (á, ā, à) • Monosyllabic lexical contours HM, HL, LH (a᷇, â, ǎ) ... M and L triggers downdrift (automatic downstep) • The pitch range of the speaker is compressed after each instance of M and L ... Otherwise • The final vowel of the subject becomes nasalized • The following word is downstepped • Is there a floating L?
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones; contours HM/HL/LH treated as lexical sequences on monosyllables. Morphologically triggered downstep (marked ꜜ) beside automatic downdrift; a floating L is raised only as a question.

sources.note: Dedicated grammatical-tone study (conference slides, not a published paper). Verbs carry lexical melodies H, HM, HL, M, L; a floating L grammatical tone (glossed apva, 'absent preverbal non-subject argument') targets the verb when no non-subject argument immediately precedes it (argued NOT to mark intransitivity): H -> LH, HM -> LHM, HL -> L, M and L unaffected after past/irrealis/evidential markers; with other auxiliaries (negative, subjunctive) H verbs are instead downstepped; realization partly lexically conditioned; analysed as a construct tune (Rolle 2018).

sources.note: Slide 5 states the Kourinion NT system: 3 flat tones H, M, L and (potentially) 3 lexical contour tones HM, ML, LH, vowel length not phonemic. The talk describes vowel prolongation with tonal modulation (LH, resolving to H, or resolving to M) in six constructions at Kourinion (identificational 'it's X', WH questions, postverbal nominal complements, future, hypothetical conditionals, an imperfective alternative) versus only the identificational construction at Djigouera, and proposes a historical source for this grammatical tone.
